title: Recursive CTEs
summary: Queries that build on their own output: number series, calendars and org charts.

steps.title: A query that calls itself
body: `WITH RECURSIVE` lets a CTE refer to **itself**. It has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`:
SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 5  -- recursive step: new rows from the previous ones

The database runs the anchor, then repeatedly runs the step on the rows produced **last time**, until a step produces nothing. The `WHERE x < 5` is what stops it: forget it and the query runs forever (SQLite will happily oblige; SQL Server stops at 100 levels by default).
Dialects: PostgreSQL, SQLite and MySQL write `WITH RECURSIVE`; SQL Server and Oracle write just `WITH`.

code: SELECT x * 2 FROM n WHERE x < 20
steps.explain: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Then 16 < 20 lets one more step run and produce 32; 32 fails the test, so the next step is empty.

steps.title: Countdown
steps.prompt: Launch day for the new season. Return a single column **x** counting down from **10 to 1**, in that order, using a recursive CTE.
solution: SELECT x - 1 FROM n WHERE x > 1
SELECT x FROM n ORDER BY x DESC;
hints: Add `ORDER BY x DESC` to make the order explicit.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a recursive CTE that returns the numbers 1 to 3.
lines: SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 3
steps.explain: Anchor first, then UNION ALL, then the recursive step with its stopping condition, then the query that reads the CTE.

steps.title: Calendars from nothing
body: Reports need a row for **every day**, even days with no sales. Generate the days:
SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE day < '2026-09-07'
LEFT JOIN purchases AS x ON x.day = d.day
`date(day, '+1 day')` is SQLite's date arithmetic. Elsewhere:
SQL Server  DATEADD(day, 1, day)  inside a recursive CTE

steps.title: Every day of the sale
prompt: Return every day from **2026-08-30** to **2026-09-07** with that day's total gems (**gems**, `0` if none), in date order.
Tables: `players(id, handle, country, joined)` and `purchases(id, player_id, item, gems, day)`.
solution: SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE day < '2026-09-07'
LEFT JOIN purchases AS x ON x.day = d.day
setup: CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, handle TEXT, country TEXT, joined TEXT);
CREATE TABLE purchases (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, player_id INTEGER REFERENCES players(id), item TEXT, gems INTEGER, day TEXT);
hints: Generate the days with a recursive CTE, then LEFT JOIN purchases.

steps.title: Walking a tree
body: `employees.manager_id` makes a tree. To find **everyone under** Marcus Bell (id 2), at any depth:
WITH RECURSIVE team(id, name, depth) AS (
SELECT id, name, 0 FROM employees WHERE id = 2          -- start at Marcus
JOIN team AS t ON e.manager_id = t.id                    -- their direct reports
Each round finds the direct reports of the people found in the previous round. It stops when a round finds nobody new.
Walk **up** instead (an employee's chain of bosses) by flipping the join: `ON e.id = t.manager_id`.

steps.prompt: How many people does this return (including Ayla herself)?
code: SELECT id FROM employees WHERE name = 'Ayla Demir'
SELECT e.id FROM employees AS e JOIN art ON e.manager_id = art.id

steps.title: Marcus's whole org
prompt: Return the **name** and **depth** (0 for Marcus Bell himself, 1 for his direct reports, and so on) of everyone in **Marcus Bell's** organisation.
Tables: `employees(id, name, title, team, manager_id, salary)`; `manager_id` points at another employee (NULL for the CEO).
solution: WITH RECURSIVE team(id, name, depth) AS (
SELECT id, name, 0 FROM employees WHERE name = 'Marcus Bell'
JOIN team AS t ON e.manager_id = t.id
setup: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, title TEXT, team TEXT, manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id), salary INTEGER);

steps.title: Chain of command
prompt: Wes Holloway wants to know who's above him. Return the **name** and **title** of everyone in his management chain, **from his direct manager up to the CEO**, in that order. Don't include Wes.
Tables: `employees(id, name, title, team, manager_id, salary)`; `manager_id` points at another employee (NULL for the CEO).
solution: WITH RECURSIVE up(id, name, title, manager_id, lvl) AS (
SELECT id, name, title, manager_id, 0 FROM employees WHERE name = 'Wes Holloway'
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.title, e.manager_id, u.lvl + 1
JOIN up AS u ON e.id = u.manager_id
SELECT name, title FROM up WHERE lvl > 0 ORDER BY lvl;
setup: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, title TEXT, team TEXT, manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id), salary INTEGER);

steps.title: Org cost
prompt: For each of the CEO's **direct reports**, return their **name** and the **total salary** of their whole organisation including themselves (**org_salary**), highest first.
Tables: `employees(id, name, title, team, manager_id, salary)`; `manager_id` points at another employee (NULL for the CEO).
solution: SELECT id, id FROM employees WHERE manager_id = 1
SELECT o.root, e.id FROM employees AS e JOIN org AS o ON e.manager_id = o.id
JOIN employees AS r ON r.id = o.root
JOIN employees AS e ON e.id = o.id
setup: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, title TEXT, team TEXT, manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id), salary INTEGER);
